title: Sous Vide Times: Thickness, Not Weight — The Baldwin Tables
h1: Sous vide time by thickness — heat diffusion, not weight
description: Sous vide cook time scales with thickness squared, not weight. A 1-inch steak needs 60 min; a 2-inch steak needs 4 hours to reach core temp.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against Douglas Baldwin's 'Practical Guide to Sous Vide Cooking' (Cooking Issues), FDA Food Code 2022 §3-401, and USDA FSIS pasteurization tables

hero: Sous vide cook time depends on thickness, not weight. A 250 g steak that is 1 inch (25 mm) thick is done in 60 minutes; a 500 g steak that is 2 inches (50 mm) thick needs about 4 hours — four times as long, because heat conduction scales with thickness squared.
body: The physics: heat diffuses into meat by conduction. The time to bring the core to within 0.5 °C of the water-bath temperature is proportional to the slab's thickness *squared* divided by thermal diffusivity (Fourier's law, ∂T/∂t = α ∇²T). Meat's diffusivity α ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻⁷ m²/s. Double the thickness and heat-up time quadruples. Weight is a red herring — a 2 kg flat brisket 25 mm thick cooks to core in the same time as a 250 g medallion of the same thickness.
## The exact model

> t (min) ≈ 6.85 × (thickness in mm)² / 1000  (Baldwin, meat, single-side approach)
> Or from the graph: 25 mm → 60 min · 40 mm → 2:30 · 50 mm → 4:00 · 60 mm → 5:45 · 70 mm → 8:00
> α (meat, cooked) ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻⁷ m²/s (Baldwin 2012, table 2.1)
## Core heat-up table (bath at target ± 0.5 °C)
Values from Baldwin's Table 2.2 for beef starting at 5 °C, bath 55–60 °C. Frozen adds ~50–70% to the time because the phase change (ice → water) consumes 334 kJ/kg of latent heat.
## Pasteurization vs heating

Reaching core temperature is not the same as being safe. USDA FSIS 2021 Appendix A gives log-10 reduction times: to achieve a 6.5-log kill of *Salmonella* in intact beef, hold at 55 °C for 89 min *after* the core hits that temperature, or 55.5 °C for 75 min, down to 60 °C for 12 min. Poultry (7-log target) at 60 °C needs 34 min hold; 65 °C needs 4 min. Total cook = heat-up time from the thickness table **plus** the required hold time.
## Worked example — 2" ribeye, medium-rare
Target: 54.5 °C (130 °F) medium-rare, safe pasteurization. Thickness 50 mm from fridge.

> Heat-up (Baldwin): 4:00 to hit 54 °C core
> Pasteurization hold at 54.5 °C for 6.5-log Salmonella (FSIS Appendix A extrapolation): ~2:30
> Total minimum: 6:30 · Practical bag time: 6:30–8:00 (texture stays fine)
> Upper limit before mushy texture (Baldwin): ~24 hours at ≤55 °C, ~8 hours at ≥58 °C
## Chicken breast at 60 °C

20 mm breast from fridge: 45 min heat-up + 34 min pasteurization hold = 79 min minimum. Practical: bag 90 min at 60 °C. Result is safe, juicy, and hits 7-log Salmonella reduction — the same target as USDA's 74 °C (165 °F) instant-kill rule but 14 °C cooler, keeping myosin denatured while actin (collagen contraction) mostly intact.
## Frozen-from-bag rule

Baldwin's rule of thumb: add 50% to the heat-up time (not the hold time) for frozen meat, provided the bath is at or below 65 °C. Above 65 °C the surface overcooks before the core thaws — sear a frozen steak instead, or thaw in the bag under running cold water for 20 minutes first.
## Fish — different diffusivity

Fish (α ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ m²/s but lower connective tissue) heats slightly faster and needs no pasteurization hold if consumed immediately. 25 mm salmon at 52 °C: 40 min heat-up, ready. Do not exceed 55 °C — myosin fibres separate and texture goes chalky.
## Measuring thickness correctly

Measure the *thickest* part with the bag flattened. Vacuum-sealed pouches compress meat by 5–10%; use the compressed dimension. For irregular cuts (bone-in short rib, chicken thigh), the bone conducts heat faster than the meat, so time to the thickest muscle section, not the bone.
## The five-second recap
Thickness, not weight. Time scales as thickness². 1 inch = 1 hour, 2 inches = 4 hours (heat-up only). Then add pasteurization hold per FSIS Appendix A if food safety matters.

faqs.a: Heat diffuses inward from all bag surfaces. Thin/wide and thick/narrow pieces of the same weight have very different core distances. Only the shortest distance to the centre matters, i.e., half-thickness for a slab.

faqs.q: Can I stack steaks in one bag?
faqs.a: No — treat the stack as one thick piece and use combined thickness. Two 25 mm steaks touching cook like one 50 mm steak (4 hours, not 1 hour).

faqs.q: Do I need to hold for pasteurization if I sear after?
faqs.a: A hard sear (30–45 s per side, 200 °C+) pasteurizes the outer millimetre only. Intact muscle (steak) is sterile inside — the sear alone is enough. Ground, injected or mechanically tenderized meat requires the FSIS hold.

Douglas Baldwin's tables are the industry reference used by Anova, Joule, ChefSteps and USDA educational materials. They come from finite-element modelling of Fourier's equation with experimental validation. Not a regulation, but the closest thing sous vide has to a standard.

faqs.q: What water bath accuracy do I need?
faqs.a: ±0.5 °C is enough for texture; ±0.1 °C matters only near thresholds (52.5 °C rare-medium boundary, 60 °C poultry safety). Anova Pro and Joule Turbo hit ±0.05 °C; cheap circulators drift ±1 °C — recalibrate against a probe thermometer.
